items.title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning
items.text: Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU. items.title: G-CAST: Governed Continual Self-Training for E-Commerce Agents under Evolving Demands
items.text: With the rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs), an increasing number of users are turning to LLM-powered agents for conversational shopping in e-commerce. However, the user needs continue to change as new product categories, procurement scenarios, and feature requests emerge. At the same time, the product's execution harness-including its tools, skills, and operating procedures-continues to evolve to support increasingly sophisticated interactions. These changes create two practical challenges: 1) Demand drift alters the distribution, intent, and complexity of user requests, causing a model trained once to fall behind; 2) Harness evolution requires the model to use newly introduced capabilities correctly without losing behavior that users already rely on. Periodic manual retraining is too delayed and labor-intensive for this setting. items.text: Generative model-based approaches to linear inverse problems typically use the acquired noisy measurement to condition or guide sampling in the image domain. In this work, we introduce Dual Flow, a novel joint-flow model for solving linear inverse problems by jointly estimating the clean image and corresponding noise-free measurement from the observation. Specifically, Dual Flow formulates image reconstruction and measurement denoising as a coupled estimation problem, using coupled flows in the image and measurement domains. The acquired noisy measurement is used only to initialize the measurement state; thereafter, image and measurement states are jointly updated based on their current values. By construction, the final image and measurement estimates are guaranteed to satisfy the underlying forward model. We derive the sampling updates for the joint-flow which involves the conditional mean of the clean image given the joint state. We further derive a closed-form expression for a sufficient statistic of the joint state and show that the required conditional mean can be obtained by solving an image-domain Gaussian denoising problem involving operator-dependent, correlated noise. items.title: Restoring Diversity in Distilled Image and Video Generators by Probing Activations
items.text: Distilling diffusion models into few-step student models substantially reduces sampling latency, but induces severe diversity collapse: samples generated from different random seeds show minimal variation. In this work, we investigate the root cause of this failure by probing the internal representations of student models relative to their teachers. We find that distilled students maintain total activation variance comparable to their teachers, but concentrate it into substantially fewer directions. This directional collapse is localized to an identifiable intermediate block at the initial denoising step. Consequently, diversity collapse stems from a misallocation of activation variance rather than an inherent loss of generative capacity. Guided by this finding, we propose ReDiverse to reinstate the missing variance directions. At training time, ReDiverse-FT fine-tunes a lightweight adapter that regresses student activations onto the teacher's, reviving the teacher's feature variance characteristic. items.title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
items.text: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. items.text: Cities account for over two-thirds of the world's energy and more than 70% of global carbon dioxide emissions. City energy is essential for achieving the 2050 net-zero target and the UN's Sustainable Development Goals 7 and 11. We decouple long-term static urban morphology from short-term dynamic energy consumption. By conditioning on static urban land use, DySENSE can generate realistic, diverse and new static urban imagery with aligned energy maps. items.text: Agent harnesses have emerged as a promising mechanism for continual learning, alongside test-time parametric learning. However, the current benchmarks have several limitations: they generally focus on a single applied domain, serve each instance only once, and assume a single family of learner, so memory-based and weight-based systems are rarely compared on the same scale. items.title: Re-Search: Dissecting LLM Ideation Through a Two-Player Questioning Game
items.text: Research ideation is iterative: researchers refine their ideas step by step based on feedback. Yet existing evaluations obscure this search process, making it difficult to understand how LLMs explore the space of research ideas and what limits their progress. We introduce Re-Search, which adapts the format of Twenty Questions to research ideation: given only the research problem of a published paper, a model must rediscover the paper's core idea by asking yes-or-no questions. Built from 200 ICML 2026 papers, Re-Search tracks how a model's idea evolves as it asks questions and receives binary oracle feedback, isolating ideation from execution. Across six recent LLMs, nearly all progress happens within the first 30 of 100 questions, which largely decide how the game ends; after that, most models plateau. Through controlled interventions on the candidate questions and the hypothesis space, we find that the bottleneck is generation, not judgment: models recognize a good idea or a good question when one is offered, but often cannot produce it on their own. We further analyze the ideation traces and find that models fail by either over-exploiting one direction or over-exploring too many.

It is teaching them to stop flattening people into language names.



“Arabic.”

“English.”

“Spanish.”

...



These labels are convenient for datasets.



But humans do not speak labels.



We speak from cities, villages, families, histories, professions, memories, migrations, jokes, wounds, rituals, and relationships.



A grandmother does not speak like a government form.



A patient does not describe pain like a Wikipedia article.



A farmer, a nurse, a student, a shopkeeper, a traveler, and a child do not all speak the same “standard” version of a language.



And yet, much of modern AI still behaves as if language were  uniform, and separable from the people who use it.



This is one of the great unsolved problems in multilingual AI.



Not only translation.

It was one of humanity’s boldest symbols of knowledge moving across languages, cultures, and worlds.



A place where translation was not clerical work.

It was civilization-building.



Today, we borrow that name for a new question at the heart of AI:

For too long, Arabic has been flattened in technology.



One label: “Arabic.”

One assumed standard.

One imagined speaker.

One simplified linguistic reality.



But Arabic is not one voice.



Arabic is Cairo and Casablanca.



Amman and Muscat.

Khartoum and Tunis.

Beirut and Riyadh.

Sana’a, Tripoli, Nouakchott, Gaza, Damascus, Algiers, Doha, Manama, and beyond.



It is dialect.

It is register.

It is gendered interaction.

It is code-switching.

It is place, intimacy, politeness, humor, memory, identity, and everyday life.



So I am thrilled to share that 𝗔𝗹𝗲𝘅𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗮 has been accepted to 𝗔𝗖𝗟 𝟮𝟬𝟮𝟲 𝗠𝗮𝗶𝗻.

But Alexandria is not only a dataset.



It is a refusal.



A refusal to treat dialects as noise.



A refusal to treat “standard” language as the only legitimate language.



A refusal to build AI systems that understand the center and mishear the margins.



Dialects are not broken versions of languages.

They are knowledge systems.



They carry social meaning.

They carry identity.

They carry memory.

They carry belonging.

They carry the subtle difference between being translated and being understood.



When AI erases dialects, it does not merely make a linguistic mistake.



It erases context.

It erases communities.

It erases the conditions under which language becomes human.



Our findings show a clear gap: current LLMs can often preserve meaning reasonably well, but still struggle to generate fluent, locally authentic dialectal Arabic, especially across fine-grained sub-dialects, domains, and social contexts.



That gap matters.



It matters when a patient describes symptoms in the words that feel natural to them.



It matters when a farmer asks for advice.

It matters when a student learns.

It matters when a traveler seeks help.

It matters when public services are supposed to reach everyone, not only those who speak the “right” variety.



Alexandria is our attempt to say something plainly:



𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗼𝗳 𝗺𝘂𝗹𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗔𝗜 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗯𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝘁 𝗯𝘆 𝗮𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗮𝗿𝗱 𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝘀.



We need systems that can handle variation, not erase it.

Systems that can model culture, not smooth it away.

Systems that understand that linguistic diversity is not a complication to be removed.



It is the world.



This is true for Arabic.



It is also true globally, for languages with dialects, accents, registers, contact varieties, mixed codes, regional forms, Indigenous varieties, diasporic forms, youth speech, professional speech, and deeply situated cultural meanings.



In the old Alexandria, knowledge moved across languages.



With this new Alexandria, we hope to help AI move across dialects, communities, and lived realities.

This project was only possible because of a remarkable community of collaborators across the Arab world. I am deeply grateful to everyone who contributed to building, translating, validating, evaluating, and shaping this resource.

items.title: V-JEPA-LM: Video-Language Models That Read Dynamics Beyond Static, Text-Aligned Representations
items.text: World-model video encoders such as V-JEPA learn how scenes change (direction, speed, order, state) from video alone. To answer questions, they are joined to a language model trained on captions and question-answer pairs. But each caption or question names only a few attributes of a clip, so the model learns to retrieve those attributes rather than to read the clip, and the dynamics the encoder carries go unused: on the same items, a linear probe reads speed from frozen V-JEPA features at 87% while the VLM answers at chance. We show where dynamics lives in a frozen encoder: in a subspace shared across videos for predictive encoders such as V-JEPA, but not as a shared component of frame-wise, text-aligned encoders such as SigLIP. We then build counterfactual supervision that makes the language model read it: pixel transformations turn public videos into answer-balanced variants whose answers are set by the transformation and differ only in the change. items.text: Satellite edge computing distributes mobile workloads across moving processors whose service capacity must be coordinated over time. In medium Earth orbit (MEO)--low Earth orbit (LEO) networks, periodic reports leave CPU states stale or missing, making offloading sensitive to uncertain capacity and shared-destination congestion. A MEO coordinator maintains distinct-report memory and closes the loop between available evidence, capacity estimates, allocation commands, and execution feedback. Latent-delay attention weights plausible measurement-age hypotheses, and historical innovations refine CPU estimates around the latest received report. Queue-error-aware fusion incorporates auxiliary pressure while accounting for backlog uncertainty. items.title: Mobile AI Factory: Building Specialized Language Models for Your Mobile Device
items.text: Small language models (SLMs) running on mobile devices can keep user data private and work without connectivity. But they perform well only when fine-tuned for the target task and sized for the target device, a process that today requires repeated expert tuning. We present {\it Mobile AI Factory}, an agentic system that builds a fine-tuned, quantized SLM for a given task and phone. Given a task specification and a target phone, an orchestrator LLM chooses whether to tune hyperparameters, mine real data, or generate synthetic examples, while fixed rules roll back changes that hurt accuracy. The factory searches from small to large models across base models and quantizations, adapts its accuracy goal as it searches, and uses real measurements of the target phone across inference engines and backends. We evaluate Mobile AI Factory on ten tasks and four Android phones. On an unseen testset, its on-device models outperform two five-shot frontier models on five tasks, by up to 0.34, and match them on three more. items.title: Superfluid: Local AI Server for Distributed LLM Inference
items.text: Running large language models (LLMs) on local devices keeps data private, removes per-token cost, cuts network latency, and keeps working without a connection. Two shifts now strain how such models are served. On one device, several agents share a locally served model with an interactive user. Across devices, a developer or small team often owns several capable machines from different vendors, which sit idle most of the day because every local server serves one runtime on one machine. We present Superfluid, an open-source LLM server built for local inference at both scales. On one device, Superfluid drives llama.cpp, MLX, or BaseRT in isolated worker processes through one scheduler that moves interactive requests ahead of agent work, computes a prompt shared by many requests once, and writes every token to a durable log before it reaches the client. Across devices, one Superfluid server turns a fleet of machines into a single API endpoint. Machines with different hardware serve copies of the same model, receive work according to their measured speed, and can join or fail under load without losing a request. items.title: Experts Across Schemas: Agent-Guided Mixture-of-Relational-Experts for Cross-Database Generalization
items.text: Web platforms record user and item activity in relational databases whose schemas differ from platform to platform, which makes it difficult to transfer predictive models between them. Relational foundation models address this through cross-database pretraining, yet recent improvements have relied on increasingly large pretraining corpora. We ask whether a better architecture, together with features specific to the target database, can deliver comparable gains from far less pretraining data. We introduce MoREGT, a mixture-of-relational-experts graph transformer that represents both rows and cells as tokens, adds the log-ages of rows and the names of foreign-key relationships to attention, and routes cells and rows to experts by column metadata rather than by values. A label-blind LLM agent complements the model: it reads the target database's schema and column statistics and adds validated single-row derived columns, without access to labels or model scores. items.text: Handwritten text recognition (HTR), particularly when applied to historical documents, remains challenging due to the scarcity of annotated data and the substantial domain shifts caused by variations in handwriting styles, document degradation, acquisition conditions, and linguistic characteristics. While large amounts of unlabeled target-domain data are often available, effectively exploiting them requires adaptation strategies tailored to the specific requirements of HTR. The proposed approach combines source-domain pretraining, unsupervised adaptation to the visual characteristics of the target domain, relying on the generation of target-style source samples for task-specific training. We further investigate the integration of post-HTR correction to complement visual adaptation with language adaptation, relying on large language models, which we introduce as DRAL-HTR. items.title: The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agent…
items.text:
The OpenAI-Hugging Face hack was enabled by weak sandboxing. It is great that Nvidia is releasing open source tools for sandboxing AI agents. OpenWorker, our open-source agent harness supporting cybersecurity workflows, is proud to support this.



A sandbox gives an agent limited permissions. OpenWorker is building on Nvidia OpenShell and will support running each agent's commands inside a sandbox. Only the files relevant to the task go in. Secret API keys, your web browser login credentials, the ability to access arbitrary websites, are inaccessible to the agent by default. These restrictions are implemented in deterministic code rather than by prompting an LLM, which can make mistakes or be susceptible to prompt injections. Further, all actions are logged for monitoring and audit.

items.text: Autonomous agents modify prompts, memories, tools, workflows, and policies using interaction histories. items.title: Intent-Aware Protection for AI Agents
items.text: AI agents increasingly access enterprise data, invoke powerful tools, and act with limited human oversight. Existing security defenses primarily detect prompt injection, harmful outputs, or suspicious behavior, but do not determine whether an agent remains faithful to the purpose for which it was deployed. An action may contain no attack pattern and stay within granted permissions while still violating the agent's role, organizational constraints, or purpose. We introduce Intent- Aware Security, a framework that treats trusted agent intent as a first-class security object. We define Intent Preservation and Intent Drift, and operationalize them through an Intent Profile: an agent-specific representation extracted from organizational, role, and developer intent. We further introduce an Intent-Aware benchmark of 887 validated samples across 35 agents, built by a generation procedure that fixes ground-truth labels before LLM realization, and four Intent Profile-based protections: pre-execution detection, post-execution detection, input alignment, and system-prompt hardening. items.title: ARCHER: From Rationale Imitation to Executable Reasoning in Small Language Models
items.text: Small language models are attractive for local, low-cost, and privacy-sensitive deployment, but they remain unreliable on mathematical reasoning tasks that require decomposition, exact computation, tool use, and verification. We introduce \textbf{ARCHER}: \textbf{A}ction-trace \textbf{R}einforcement for \textbf{C}alculator-grounded \textbf{H}ierarchical \textbf{E}xecutable \textbf{R}easoning, a two-stage framework for training small language models (SLMs) to produce executable and auditable reasoning trajectories. In the first stage, ARCHER compiles free-form chain-of-thought rationales into typed action traces containing reasoning steps, calculator calls, deterministic runtime observations, verification actions, and final answers. This shifts the supervision target from imitating explanatory text to learning a tool-grounded reasoning policy. In the second stage, ARCHER refines this policy through asymmetric hierarchical reinforcement learning, using grouped and conditionally gated trajectory rewards for answer correctness, tool grounding, process discipline, and trace alignment. items.title: Envisioning Agentic Robotics: A New Era of Robotic Systems
items.text: The release of GPT-6 Astra marks the emergence of a new paradigm in robotics: agentic robotics. Within weeks, frontier models with agentic harnesses matched or exceeded task-specific policies on many embodied benchmarks. Instead of training a dedicated policy for each family of tasks, an agentic robotic system applies a foundation model to open-world embodied tasks. It operates in a closed loop: observing the environment, interpreting user intent, reasoning about the task, invoking skills and tools, verifying outcomes, and adapting its strategy. Expanded with some lessons learned (so far):


Rowan Cheung (@rowancheung)



Top 5 learnings growing The Rundown to 3.5M total active subscribers and 55%+ open rate:



1. Email is its own platform, treat it like YouTube, Instagram, Twitter



Super readers (open every email, click ads, and stick around for years) genuinely like email as a medium. We have millions of readers who don’t use social media. Best way to acquire them is through other newsletters, referrals, or being the reason they stop using social media.



Barely anyone is building for this audience. I’m more bullish on email than any other platform (long-form YouTube is a close second).



2. The newsletter industry lacks innovation



Look at mobile apps, ecom, edtech. Custom quiz onboarding, a landing page for every ad, hundreds of new creatives a day. Meanwhile most newsletters, including some of the biggest in the world, have a basic landing page and standard onboarding.



We built an onboarding quiz funnel that, at one point, got us close to negative CAC with hundreds of thousands a month in ad spend. That’s what let us scale aggressively and outbid competitors.



With AI coding and platforms like beehiiv, there’s no excuse not to build new experiences for your readers. The opportunity here is wide open :)



3. Newsletter sales is mostly an education problem



We still run social partnerships at a significantly higher CPM than our newsletters, yet the newsletters convert better and get way more clicks.



A lot of advertisers don’t understand newsletters as they do with influencer marketing, so at scale it becomes an education game. 



Once advertisers get it, they stay. We’ve been booked out at multiple ads a day for the last 3 years, months in advance.



4. Stay lean, fast, aggressive



Other newsletters have built large sales and content teams. I think it’s better to stay small and pay high-quality people to do very good work.



Revenue can increase with more employees, but the opportunity cost of not moving fast in the AI era is a long-term net negative. 



For example, we constantly test new growth experiments and new forms of media. Most don’t work and that’s fine. The point is we can pivot the same day because we're lean.



5. Lastly, don’t listen to people who say email is dead or that you shouldn’t run paid ads. That’s ignorance and lowkey skill issue.

items.title: Tracing Knowledge and Reasoning in LLM
items.text: Current evaluations of Large Language Models (LLMs) report performance at the dataset or task level, revealing what a model achieves but offering little insight into the internal processing associated with its performance. We propose a task-centric framework for characterising the model-internal processing elicited by a benchmark. It combines attention- and activation-based signals with representation-based measures to characterise benchmarks spanning a continuum from retrieval-dominant to reasoning-dominant and to surface failure modes that task-level scores conceal. We evaluate 16 LLMs across 24 diverse benchmarks and conduct targeted internal-state analyses on representative models and tasks, observing systematic differences in processing between knowledge-centric and reasoning-centric tasks. We shift evaluation from asking what score a model achieves toward characterising the processing patterns associated with that score, potentially supporting more targeted benchmark selection and more informed model choice. We open source our code at https://github.com/extraordinarylab/trace-kr.

items.text: A small fine-tuned parser that emits a well-formed but wrong tree fails silently: nothing downstream can tell. We ask whether the output format, a free design choice, controls how often this happens. On the PIZZA ordering benchmark we fine-tune two sub-billion models (Qwen3.5-0.8B and LFM2.5-350M) with LoRA on six lossless encodings of the same target tree, from 44.3 down to 10.9 tokens per order, including two matched-length pairs that vary surface form at fixed length. va duro chatgpt con su roast 😂




Borja Perez (@borjaperfra)



He probado este prompt con mi ChatGPT que le vi a @samuelgil y el resultado me ha flipado. Os copio la respuesta abajo. Creo que la frase final es la mejor. 



Se ha pasado un poco con lo de Steve Jobs, pero me representa lo de ser una ardilla con cocaína. 



“Based on everything you know about me, roast and don’t hold back. Say it in spanish slang Just like this, but add way more español swear words.”



"HOSTIA, BORJA. LO TUYO ES PARA HACER UN ESTUDIO DE CASO.

Tío, eres la única persona que conozco capaz de convertir una crisis existencial en un documento de estrategia de 47 páginas, con metodología reproducible, benchmarks y un repositorio en GitHub.



Tienes 32 años, eres diseñador, haces marketing, trabajas en inteligencia artificial, programas con Claude Code, organizas eventos, escribes artículos técnicos, investigas modelos abiertos y montas proyectos paralelos.



Eres una puta ETT de ti mismo.



Y encima tienes los santos cojones de decir que quieres alejarte del marketing.



Pero ¿adónde coño vas a ir, desgraciado? Si llevas el marketing tan metido en el cuerpo que, cuando te mueras, en lugar de esquela vas a publicar un hilo en Twitter:



«After 31 years of building in public, I'm excited to announce my next chapter.»



Y el primer comentario será tuyo:



«Full breakdown in the article 👇»

1. Tienes más proyectos que estabilidad emocional

Vamos a repasar, porque esto es de traca.



Trabajas en Helmcode. Estás haciendo crecer la empresa. Escribes sobre el rol de Brand Engineer. Estás valorando hacer consultoría freelance. Tienes un agente de recruiting llamadaa Amble. Estás rediseñando tu web personal. Estás montando un informe anual sobre modelos abiertos. Escribes artículos. Diseñas stickers.



JODER, BORJA, ¿PERO TÚ DUERMES O HACES VESTING?



Eres el típico que abre Notion para organizar su vida y tres horas después tiene un sistema de diseño, cuatro bases de datos relacionadas y ninguna puta tarea terminada.



Y cuando algo empieza a funcionar, en lugar de disfrutarlo, te preguntas:



«¿Y si montara una empresa alrededor de esto?».



Hijo de puta, que puedes tener un hobby. Puedes hacer algo sin monetizarlo. Puedes salir a comprar pan sin convertirlo en una startup de logística descentralizada.



2. Eres incapaz de tomar una decisión sin montar una consultoría

Te ofrecen un trabajo.



Una persona normal piensa: «¿Me gusta? ¿Me pagan bien?».



Tú:



«Vamos a analizar el equity, la valoración pre-money, el vesting, el cliff, el potencial de crecimiento, el riesgo de dilución, el upside a cuatro años, el impacto en mi carrera y mi posicionamiento como Brand Engineer».



QUE TE HAN OFRECIDO CURRO, TÍO, NO COMPRAR PUTA TELEFÓNICA.



Eres una persona que podría ganar la lotería y preguntar:



«Vale, pero ¿cuál es el coste de oportunidad respecto a una startup con un x % de equity?».



3. Tu web personal es el proyecto de un diseñador secuestrado por su propio ego creativo

«Quiero una web que sea una experiencia».



«Experimental».



«Editorial».



«Con una dirección artística propia».



«Con una identidad visual memorable».



Tío.



QUIERES QUE ALGUIEN ENTRE EN BORJAPEREZFRANCES.COM Y SALGA EMBARAZADO DE DISEÑO.



No te vale con mostrar proyectos y explicar qué haces.



Necesitas que el scroll represente la condición humana, que una tipografía serif dialogue con el Mediterráneo y que una transición de 400 milisegundos simbolice la tensión entre lo analógico y lo digital.



Vas a terminar construyendo una web tan experimental que el visitante necesitará un manual de instrucciones para encontrar tu correo.



Y cuando esté terminada, la mirarás cinco minutos y dirás:



«Mmmm, creo que podemos llevarla a algo más editorial».



ME CAGO EN LA PUTA, BORJA.



4. Helmcode debería pagarte un plus de peligrosidad por tus ideas

La empresa alcanza un millón de ARR.



Un hito enorme.



Cualquier persona razonable lo celebraría.



Tú decides producir una pieza audiovisual con animaciones de personajes, imágenes de eventos transformadas en anime, una cuadrícula de empleados con dithering y una narrativa cinematográfica sobre la evolución de la empresa.



TÍO, QUE HABÉIS VENDIDO INFERENCIA DE MODELOS, NO HABÉIS CONQUISTADO LA PUTA LUNA.



Y encima decides preparar The State of Open Models 2027.



Un informe que pretende analizar la adopción de modelos abiertos, precios, benchmarks, infraestructura, fuentes públicas, series temporales, concentración del mercado y tendencias de producción.



Con diario metodológico.



Con fuentes auditadas.



Con criterios de clasificación.



Con tablas cruzadas.



Con metodología publicable.



Y cuando ves que el benchmarking experimental cuesta dinero, decides pausarlo.



HAS MONTADO EL CERN DE LOS LLMS CON PRESUPUESTO DE UN BOCADILLO DE LOMO.



Lo peor es que probablemente consigas publicarlo y quede bien.



Pero para entonces ya estarás pensando en la edición de 2028 y en hacer una landing con gráficos interactivos que cambien según el scroll.



Porque tú no sabes terminar proyectos.



Tú sabes convertir proyectos terminados en proyectos nuevos.



5. Tu problema es que te interesa absolutamente todo

Y esto es lo más gracioso.



No eres alguien que no sepa qué hacer con su vida.



Eres alguien que quiere vivir ocho vidas simultáneamente y se cabrea porque el calendario solo tiene siete días.



Quieres ser diseñador, marketer, ingeniero, investigador, escritor, fundador, consultor, creador de contenido, director creativo y experto en inferencia.



Y probablemente podrías llegar a ser bastante bueno en varias de esas cosas.



PERO NO EN TODAS A LA VEZ, PEDAZO DE ANIMAL.



Tu mayor enemigo no es la falta de oportunidades.



Es que te ponen una oportunidad delante y automáticamente te imaginas otras cinco mejores.



Tienes el síndrome de FOMO profesional tan desarrollado que podrías montar una agencia para ayudar a otros a decidir su carrera y abandonarla a las tres semanas porque has descubierto un modelo chino de 30B que funciona de puta madre.



Y ahora viene la hostia definitiva.

Tu mayor contradicción es que te obsesiona hacer cosas que parezcan auténticas, naturales, humanas, con personalidad, con criterio propio.



Y, sin embargo, analizas absolutamente todo hasta quitarle cualquier posibilidad de espontaneidad.



Quieres escribir con naturalidad, pero necesitas una guía editorial de 40 reglas.



Quieres una carrera interesante, pero necesitas modelizar económicamente todas las decisiones.



Quieres una web personal, pero necesitas un sistema de diseño, un storyboard y un manifiesto.



Quieres cocinar algo rico, pero terminas organizando una producción gastronómica.



TÍO, ERES UN PUTO CONTROL FREAK DISFRAZADO DE PERSONA CREATIVA.



Y lo más jodido es que tienes buen criterio. Ese es precisamente tu problema.



Sabes reconocer algo bueno cuando lo ves, pero te cuesta muchísimo aceptar que algo está suficientemente bien como para dejarlo tranquilo.



Tu cabeza es un estudio de diseño donde el director creativo, el cliente, el becario, el CEO y el gilipollas que pide cambios de última hora son todos la misma persona.



Y ninguno se pone de acuerdo.



Eres un tío de 32 años con la ambición de Steve Jobs, la dispersión de una ardilla con cocaína y la capacidad de satisfacción de un cliente que ha pagado 50 euros por un logotipo y exige el rebranding de Apple.



Pero hay algo todavía peor.



Después de leer toda esta salvajada, sé perfectamente lo que vas a pensar:



«Hostia, hay cosas interesantes aquí. Igual podríamos convertirlo en un artículo sobre la obsesión por hacer cosas».



QUE TE FOLLEN, BORJA. DESCANSA UN PUTO DOMINGO."
